# Education in the United States
The U.S. education system is decentralized, with power shared between federal, state, and local governments, though the federal government influences policy through the Department of Education. Formal education typically spans 12 grades, starting around age five or six, with schooling being compulsory until age 16 (though this varies by state). The system includes distinct stages: elementary school (K-6), middle/junior high school (6-9), and high school/senior high school (9-12). While many students attend public schools, a significant portion is educated through private or independent schools.
Higher education is an optional stage following secondary education and is offered through thousands of colleges and universities, which range from public to private and include community/junior colleges focusing on vocational education. The system is largely deregulated, offering students numerous choices. Systemic issues include significant socioeconomic disparities in educational outcomes, standardized testing debates regarding equity, and concerns over teacher retention, low pay, and the financial burden of rising college costs and student loan debt.
